notes.meaning: The psalmist calls on God as the one to whom vengeance belongs. Here vengeance means God's fair justice, which gives everyone what they are due. It is not angry, spiteful revenge like ours. "Shine forth" asks God to show himself openly as Judge. Because vengeance belongs to God, we should not take revenge ourselves but leave it with him.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think the psalm was written long after David, perhaps in the later Persian period. They treat the old Greek title that names David as unreliable.

notes.meaning: God is the Judge of the whole earth, and no one is outside his rule. "Rise up" asks him to take his seat as Judge and act. "Render a reward to the proud" means paying them back for their pride and the harm they have done. Wanting this kind of justice is right when it comes from love of what is right and pity for victims, not from personal revenge.

"How long?" is the cry of God's suffering people in every age. It is repeated because the wicked boast day after day. The psalmist does not doubt that God is just. He only wonders how long the dark night will last. The triumph of the wicked has limits and will come to an end.

The wicked pour out proud words the way a fountain pours out water: freely and without stopping. Their speech is harsh and insulting toward God and his people, and they brag as if no one can call them to account. A day of reckoning is coming for all such hard words.

The wicked crush God's people. "Your heritage" means the same thing: God's own people, whom he treasures as his special possession. The psalmist pleads, in effect, "Lord, they are yours. Will you let them be trampled?" If God's people suffered like this then, we should not be surprised when it happens now.

The widow, the foreigner and the orphan were the weakest people, with no one to defend them. God's law gave them special care. These oppressors pick on them and even kill them. Justice for the weak is a mark of good government, and harming them is a mark of the very worst.

The oppressors tell themselves that God does not see or care. That belief is what makes them so bold. They act blindly because they imagine a blind God. Calling him "the God of Jacob" makes their claim even more foolish, since this is the God who has cared for his people again and again.

The psalmist turns and speaks to the foolish. "Senseless" means brutish, like animals without understanding. Some read this as aimed at the godless oppressors. Others see it as aimed at people among God's own people who were starting to doubt because God's justice seemed slow. Either way, no one is too foolish to be urged to become wise.

The argument is simple. The God who made the ear can surely hear, and the God who shaped the eye can surely see. Whatever is good in what he made must be in him in a far greater way. The verse does not say God has ears or eyes like ours. It only says he hears and sees, because God is spirit and has no body.

God disciplines whole nations for their sins. So he will surely deal with these oppressors too. And since all human knowledge comes from God, he must know everything. In Hebrew the last question breaks off without its ending, as if the answer were too plain to need saying.

God knows not only what people do but also what they think, and he knows those thoughts are futile, empty as a breath. Paul quotes this verse in 1 Corinthians 3:20. Since God takes notice of our thoughts, we should guard them carefully.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The Hebrew could also be read "for they (people) are a breath," meaning people themselves are empty, not just their thoughts.

notes.meaning: The tone changes from complaint to quiet faith. God allows his people to suffer as a loving father trains his child. "Discipline" here means that kind of loving correction. It is the teaching from God's word that comes with the trouble that does us good. Trouble on its own does not. So the person God disciplines and teaches is truly blessed.

God's teaching gives his people inner rest and calm during hard days, so that they are not crushed or tempted to give up. Meanwhile, God is preparing a pit, a trap, into which the wicked will fall. So we can wait patiently and need not rush to see them punished.
God will never abandon his people, because they belong to him. They may be cast down, but they will never be cast off. Paul drew comfort from this same truth in Romans 11:1.

Things that now seem upside down will be set right again. Justice will return to what is righteous, either in this life or at the final judgment. Then all who are honest at heart will gladly welcome it and follow it with praise.

The psalmist looks around for someone to stand up for him against evil people, and he finds no one. The questions show that only God will help. Having no human helper drives the heart to rest on the Lord alone.
"The abode of silence" means the grave. Without the Lord's help, the psalmist would soon have died. His own past experience proves that God is the one who helps.

Just when he felt himself falling, God's loving devotion held him up, like a prop that keeps something from toppling over. It was God's mercy that saved him, not his own strength. We are ready for this help when we admit our weakness and tell God our foot is slipping.

His anxious thoughts were tangled and tossed about, like branches in the wind. In the middle of them, God's comfort did more than calm him. It delighted his soul. These comforts are God's promises, his word, his Spirit, and the memory of his past kindness.

A "corrupt throne" means unjust rulers or judges. Such rulers make wrong legal by passing laws for it. God will never be their partner or approve them. Daniel's enemies did this when they passed a law against prayer. Wrong is not made right by being made law.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some translate "by decree" as "against the law," meaning these rulers act contrary to what is right.

notes.meaning: The wicked gang up on good people and sentence the innocent to death, often while pretending to follow the law. Daniel's enemies did exactly this. Some older Christian writers also saw this verse pictured in the unjust trial of Jesus.

However many enemies gather, the Lord is the psalmist's fortress. A "rock of refuge" pictures the natural rock strongholds of Israel's hills, where people could hide safely out of reach. Here the psalmist tells, from his own life, how God has kept him.

God will turn the wicked's own evil back on them. The harm they planned for others will fall on themselves. The repeated line, "The LORD our God will destroy them," shows how certain this is, and it echoes the repeated cry in verse 1. As surely as his people can call him "our God," he will set things right.
